verses.1: The LORD provided a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah remained in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights.
verses.2: Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish.
verses.3: He said, "I called out in my distress to the LORD, and he answered me from the depths of Sheol. I cried, and you heard my voice."
verses.4: You had cast me into the heart of the seas, and rivers encircled me. All your waves and breakers passed over me.
verses.5: I thought, 'I am cut off from your sight,' yet I will still look again toward your holy temple.
verses.6: Waters surrounded me to the very core; the deep encircled me, and the sea blocked the light from my head.
verses.7: I descended to the roots of the mountains. The earth barred me in forever, but you brought my life up from the pit, O LORD my God.
verses.8: When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.
verses.9: Those who cling to worthless things abandon their loyalty.
verses.10: But I, with a voice of thanksgiving and praise, will offer sacrifice to you, as I have vowed, I will repay my vow of salvation to the LORD."
verses.11: The LORD then gave a command to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto the dry land.

notes:
Notes
- v. 5: "I will still look again" — the Hebrew uses "ach" ("but") with a negative, here rendered as a contrastive "yet."
- v. 7: "the roots of the mountains" — the phrase "lekitzav ha-harim" is literally "to the bars of the mountains," but the metaphor of being buried deep is more natural in English.
- v. 9: "clinging to worthless things" — the phrase "mishmerim ha-vel shav" is literally "keepers of lies and falsehood," but the metaphor is better expressed as "those who cling to worthless things."
- v. 10: "I will repay my vow of salvation" — the Hebrew uses "yeshuat" in the construct, meaning "vow of salvation," which is rendered to capture the poetic structure.
raw:
[1] The LORD provided a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah remained in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights.

[2] Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish.

[3] He said, "I called out in my distress to the LORD, and he answered me from the depths of Sheol. I cried, and you heard my voice."

[4] You had cast me into the heart of the seas, and rivers encircled me. All your waves and breakers passed over me.

[5] I thought, 'I am cut off from your sight,' yet I will still look again toward your holy temple.

[6] Waters surrounded me to the very core; the deep encircled me, and the sea blocked the light from my head.

[7] I descended to the roots of the mountains. The earth barred me in forever, but you brought my life up from the pit, O LORD my God.

[8] When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.

[9] Those who cling to worthless things abandon their loyalty.

[10] But I, with a voice of thanksgiving and praise, will offer sacrifice to you, as I have vowed, I will repay my vow of salvation to the LORD."

[11] The LORD then gave a command to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto the dry land.

---
Notes
- v. 5: "I will still look again" — the Hebrew uses "ach" ("but") with a negative, here rendered as a contrastive "yet."
- v. 7: "the roots of the mountains" — the phrase "lekitzav ha-harim" is literally "to the bars of the mountains," but the metaphor of being buried deep is more natural in English.
- v. 9: "clinging to worthless things" — the phrase "mishmerim ha-vel shav" is literally "keepers of lies and falsehood," but the metaphor is better expressed as "those who cling to worthless things."
- v. 10: "I will repay my vow of salvation" — the Hebrew uses "yeshuat" in the construct, meaning "vow of salvation," which is rendered to capture the poetic structure.
